title: 初值定理与终值定理
statement: 图示电路中 v_s = 10u(t) V，R_1 = 2 Ω，R_2 = 3 Ω，L = 1 H，t < 0 时电路无储能。i_L、v_L 的参考方向如图。
可以求得 I_L(s) = \frac{6}{s(s + 1.2)} A·s。不做反变换，用初值定理和终值定理求 i_L(0₊)、v_L(0₊) 和 i_L(∞)。再求 I_L(s) 除 s = 0 外的极点。

questions.explain: sI_L(s) = 6/(s + 1.2) → 6/1.2 = 5 A（s → 0）。sI_L(s) 的极点 −1.2 在左半平面，终值定理适用。直流稳态下电感短路，i_L = 10/2 = 5 A，结果一致。

questions.ask: I_L(s) 除 s = 0 外的极点 p = ?
若某响应的象函数 F(s) = 1/(s² + 4)，能否用终值定理求 f(∞)？
choices: 不能：极点 ±j2 在虚轴上，f(t) = 0.5 sin 2t 没有终值
不能：因为 F(s) 没有零点
choiceExplain: 形式上算出 0，但 f(t) = 0.5 sin 2t 并不趋于 0——终值定理的条件不满足时结果没有意义。
F(0) 不是终值；终值是 sF(s) 在 s → 0 时的极限，而且这里本来就不存在。
能否用终值定理看的是极点位置，与有没有零点无关。
questions.explain: 终值定理要求 sF(s) 的极点都在左半平面（s = 0 处至多一个单极点被 s 抵消）。1/(s² + 4) 的极点 ±j2 在虚轴上，f(t) = 0.5 sin 2t 一直振荡。

hints: 初值定理：f(0₊) = lim_{s→∞} sF(s)；终值定理：f(∞) = lim_{s→0} sF(s)（sF(s) 的极点要在左半平面）。
v_L 的象函数：V_L(s) = sL·I_L(s) − L·i_L(0₋)。
把 I_L(s) 写成 V_s(s) 乘一个网络函数：分母 R_eq + sL，R_eq 是从电感看进去的等效电阻。
solution: **1. 运算电路。** V_s(s) = 10/s。从电感两端看进去，把其余部分化成戴维宁等效：V_oc(s) = \frac{10}{s}·\frac{3}{5} = 6/s，R_eq = 2∥3 = 1.2 Ω。所以 I_L(s) = \frac{6/s}{1.2 + s} = \frac{6}{s(s + 1.2)}。

en.title: Initial- and final-value theorems
statement: v_s = 10u(t) V, R_1 = 2 Ω, R_2 = 3 Ω, L = 1 H, and the circuit stores no energy for t < 0. The reference directions of i_L and v_L are as drawn.
One finds I_L(s) = \frac{6}{s(s + 1.2)} A·s. Without inverting it, use the initial- and final-value theorems to find i_L(0+), v_L(0+) and i_L(∞). Then find the pole of I_L(s) other than s = 0.

questions.explain: sI_L(s) = 6/(s + 1.2) → 0 (s → ∞). It agrees with the switching rule i_L(0+) = i_L(0−) = 0.
V_L(s) = sL·I_L(s) − L·i_L(0−) = 6/(s + 1.2), sV_L(s) = 6s/(s + 1.2) → 6 V. At 0+ the inductor is an open circuit and v_L = 10 × 3/(2 + 3) = 6 V — the same.

sI_L(s) = 6/(s + 1.2) → 6/1.2 = 5 A (s → 0). The pole −1.2 of sI_L(s) is in the left half-plane, so the final-value theorem applies. In the DC steady state the inductor is a short and i_L = 10/2 = 5 A — the same.

questions.ask: The pole p of I_L(s) other than s = 0 = ?
questions.explain: I_L(s)/V_s(s) = \frac{R_2/(R_1 + R_2)}{R_{eq} + sL} with R_eq = R_1∥R_2 = 1.2 Ω: the pole is p = −R_eq/L = −1.2 1/s (time constant τ = 1/1.2 s).

questions.ask: If a response has F(s) = 1/(s² + 4), can the final-value theorem give f(∞)?
questions.explain: The final-value theorem needs all poles of sF(s) in the left half-plane (a single pole of F at s = 0 is cancelled by the s). 1/(s² + 4) has poles ±j2 on the jω axis and f(t) = 0.5 sin 2t keeps oscillating.
choices: No: the poles ±j2 lie on the jω axis; f(t) = 0.5 sin 2t has no final value
No, because F(s) has no zeros
choiceExplain: The formula gives 0, but f(t) = 0.5 sin 2t does not tend to 0 — when the conditions fail the result is meaningless.
F(0) is not the final value; the final value is the limit of sF(s) as s → 0, and here it does not exist anyway.
Whether the theorem applies depends on the pole locations, not on zeros.

hints: Initial-value theorem: f(0+) = lim_{s→∞} sF(s); final-value theorem: f(∞) = lim_{s→0} sF(s) (the poles of sF(s) must be in the left half-plane).
The transform of v_L is V_L(s) = sL·I_L(s) − L·i_L(0−).
Write I_L(s) as V_s(s) times a network function: its denominator is R_eq + sL, with R_eq the resistance seen by the inductor.
solution: **1. s-domain circuit.** V_s(s) = 10/s. Reduce the rest of the circuit, seen from the inductor, to its Thévenin equivalent: V_oc(s) = \frac{10}{s}·\frac{3}{5} = 6/s, R_eq = 2∥3 = 1.2 Ω. So I_L(s) = \frac{6/s}{1.2 + s} = \frac{6}{s(s + 1.2)}.
**2. Initial values.** **i_L(0+) = lim sI_L(s) = 0**; V_L(s) = sI_L(s) − 0 = 6/(s + 1.2), **v_L(0+) = lim sV_L(s) = 6 V**.
**3. Final value.** **i_L(∞) = lim_{s→0} 6/(s + 1.2) = 5 A** (the pole −1.2 is in the left half-plane, so the theorem applies).
**Check:** the three-element method in the time domain gives i_L(0+) = 0, i_L(∞) = 10/2 = 5 A, τ = L/R_eq = 1/1.2 s — the same ✓.
